I have always been drawn to the places that are not quite places at all. Train stations at midnight, hospital waiting rooms, the fluorescent-lit corridors of airports, the bench outside a closed bakery in the early morning. These are thresholds, zones of suspension where no one is officially allowed to live, only to pass through. And yet, if you watch long enough, you realize people do live there, in a small and stubborn way, with their thermoses and paperbacks and half-finished crossword puzzles. I think I have spent more of my life learning who I am in those in-between hours than in any destination I was supposedly traveling toward.

Waiting does something peculiar to time. In ordinary life, we carve time into tasks: make coffee, answer email, arrive at noon. In a waiting room, time refuses to be carved. It stretches and pools and then, all at once, lurches forward when a name is called or a departure board flickers. I once spent six hours in the overnight terminal in Chicago because of snow, and I can still remember the exact pattern of the carpet, the hum of the vending machine, the way a man's shoes squeaked every time he paced past the help desk. I cannot remember the name of the hotel I stayed in the next night, or the restaurant where I ate the following day.

Perhaps that is why I like to watch people in those liminal spaces. Stripped of their usual context, strangers become briefly, wonderfully legible. The woman who is quietly rehearsing a speech to an empty seat, moving her hands in small emphatic gestures. The teenager asleep upright with his backpack still on, hugging it like a pillow, like a shield. The couple arguing in whispers, not looking at each other, because the whole terminal is watching and they know it. Everyone is performing a version of themselves that is both more honest and more theatrical than usual, because the ordinary rules of social life have been suspended. You are not expected to be efficient or productive here. You are only expected to be present, and that simple requirement makes people oddly tender toward one another.

I am not a patient person by nature. I check my phone, I refresh the departure board, I rehearse what I will say when I finally get where I am going. I make lists in my head of all the things I will do once the waiting is over, as if productivity can somehow cancel out the lost hours. This is, I know, a kind of superstition. But I have also come to suspect that the waiting is not an interruption of life but one of its purest forms. There is nothing to optimize, nothing to win. There is only the fact of being somewhere you did not choose to be, for longer than you intended, and deciding what to do with that fact.

The best waiting places understand this. They do not try to distract you with screaming televisions or forced cheerfulness. They give you a decent chair, a window, a little light that falls at the right angle in the afternoon. They let you look outside. I think of a small bus depot in the mountains where I once waited out a thunderstorm, watching rain hammer the tin roof so loudly that conversation was impossible. We all sat in silence, a dozen strangers, listening to the weather do its enormous work. No one complained. When the rain stopped, we got up slowly, as if we had been in church, and boarded the bus with a kind of newfound gentleness toward one another and toward the road ahead.

Memory, I have learned, is not a filing cabinet. It is more like a shoreline, constantly eroding and rebuilding itself around whatever happens to wash up that day. The things I thought I would remember forever slip away, and the things I barely noticed at the time rise up, sharp and detailed, years later when I least expect them. A song heard through a cracked speaker. The particular weight of a borrowed coat. The way light hit a particular wall at 4:47 in the afternoon, for no reason at all. Waiting rooms are full of such unimportant details, and I think that is why they stay with us. We are not trying to make memories there. We are trying to get somewhere else.

I do not know when I started thinking of waiting as a practice rather than a problem. Maybe it was after my father died, and I found myself in a series of actual waiting rooms, the kind with bad coffee and pamphlets about grief that no one ever reads. There, waiting was not about a delayed train. It was about learning to sit inside a question that had no answer coming. The nurse would call a name, and someone else's life would change, and the rest of us would practice, again, the terrible human art of remaining seated. I remember thinking, with a kind of irritation at my own sentimentality, that this was not the way I had imagined learning patience. I had imagined something more dignified, perhaps involving mountains or long walks. Instead, it was plastic chairs and fluorescent lights and the courage it takes not to check your phone for the hundredth time. And yet, that is where I learned it, or began to. To wait well is not to wait cheerfully, or to pretend you are not waiting at all. It is to notice the carpet, and the hum, and the people you will never see again, and to let them be enough for the length of an afternoon. It is to accept that arrival, when it comes, will not retroactively justify the hours spent getting there. The hours were their own thing, and they were, in their quiet way, a life for now.
